title: Psychiatry's diagnostic bible is finally getting a biological upgrade
gist: The American Psychiatric Association is preparing to modernize the DSM (its core diagnostic manual, last revised 2013) by incorporating neurobiology for the first time, driven by advances in Alzheimer's blood biomarkers, inflammatory markers like CRP in depression, and polygenic risk scores — a shift a DSM strategic committee member says points toward psychiatry entering an era of precision medicine.

insights.claim: There are currently no scientifically valid biomarkers for any psychiatric condition except for certain proteins used to diagnose Alzheimer's disease, a stark contrast to the rest of medicine, which routinely uses biomarkers like hemoglobin A1C for diabetes or cholesterol for cardiovascular risk.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Frames psychiatry as a large, underserved medical field for biomarker diagnostics innovation — a whitespace opportunity for diagnostics companies given nearly every other major disease category already has established biomarker tests.
insights.quote: There are currently no scientifically valid biomarkers for any psychiatric condition, with the exception of certain proteins used to diagnose Alzheimer's disease.
insights.locator: section 'Why aren't there biomarkers for mental illness?'

insights.claim: In March 2025, the FDA approved a blood test to detect amyloid and tau proteins to help confirm Alzheimer's diagnosis, replacing reliance on medical history, exam, and postmortem evidence — described as the first biomarker instance for a disorder affecting both brain and behavior.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-approved diagnostic (FDA blood test for amyloid/tau) demonstrates biomarker-based psychiatric/neurological diagnostics are commercially viable now, not just theoretical — relevant to Alzheimer's diagnostics and adjacent neuro-biomarker companies.

insights.claim: Approximately 30 percent of patients with depression have elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, suggesting CRP could serve as a biomarker to identify a depression subtype that responds better to certain treatments than patients with lower CRP levels.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: A quantified biomarker prevalence figure (30% of depression patients) for CRP-based treatment stratification, relevant to companies developing depression subtyping diagnostics or anti-inflammatory psychiatric therapeutics.
insights.quote: Approximately 30 percent of patients with depression have high CRP levels, suggesting that it may serve as a biomarker to identify a subtype of patients who may respond better to certain types of treatment.

insights.claim: Researchers are developing polygenic risk scores that bundle multiple individual genetic risk variants into a cumulative estimate of mental disorder risk, though the author notes these genetic biomarkers are 'not ready for use in the clinic' yet.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Polygenic risk scoring for psychiatric conditions is an emerging but pre-clinical diagnostic category worth tracking as genetic testing companies expand into behavioral health risk assessment.

insights.claim: The author argues that psychiatric disorders are conceptualized as overlapping behavioral syndromes rather than discrete illnesses (e.g., anxiety and mood disorders, or schizophrenia and bipolar disorder with psychosis frequently co-occur), making a single biomarker per diagnosis category an unrealistic near-term goal.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for how quickly psychiatric biomarker diagnostics can mature — the syndrome-overlap problem means single-biomarker tests are unlikely to replace clinical diagnosis wholesale in the near term, a caution against overhyping precision-psychiatry timelines.
insights.quote: Finding a single biomarker that reflects multiple processes at the same time is unrealistic.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Characterizing each of these disorders'

insights.claim: A 2013 survey of psychiatry colleagues found 65 percent predicted the DSM-6 would include laboratory tests to diagnose psychiatric disorders, and 13 years later the author (a DSM strategic committee member) confirms that integration work is only now beginning.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Shows the actual pace of institutional adoption of psychiatric biomarkers has lagged expert expectations by well over a decade — useful calibration for how long regulatory/institutional adoption of novel diagnostics can take even when experts anticipate it early.

insights.claim: The author, a DSM strategic committee member (2024-2026) on the neurobiology integration subcommittee, envisions a future where patients bring genetic tests, brain scans, and blood work into psychiatric visits for more precise, personalized diagnosis and treatment.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: An insider's stated long-term vision for precision psychiatry, useful as a directional signal for where psychiatric diagnostics R&D and clinical practice may be headed, though explicitly framed as aspirational ('the dream I have') rather than a near-term forecast.
insights.quote: That's the dream I have for the future of psychiatry.
